The installer rewrites MCP tool-name placeholders (`{{tool:list_agents}}`, `{{tools:agent-coord}}`) per harness, so committed field cards stay harness-neutral.\n\n<!-- §fleet -->\n## Fleet Bootstrap & Layout\n\nEvery project fleet starts the same way, with the same window names, geography and colors — so anyone (David or an agent glancing at a screen) can read any fleet at sight. This is canonical: don't improvise per-project layouts.\n\n**Standard window layout** (role-named windows; agreed with the console's `provision.ts` 2026-08-22 — one scheme, two implementations):\n\n```text\n<project>-coordinator   one pane (your --self-coordinator pane, renamed)\n<project>-aide          one pane\n<project>-qa            one pane\n<project>-ci            one pane (absent when the fleet runs without ci)\n<project>-workers       N even vertical panes (worker-1 … worker-N)\n```\n\nWindow names carry the plain project (windows are per-machine, like rooms); agent ids and worktrees keep the `<project>-<owner>` fleet prefix. A consumer must not assume all five windows exist — optional roles simply have no window.\n\n**Role → color map** (applied twice: tmux pane-border title color, and `/color` inside each Claude session):\n\n| Role | Color |\n|---|---|\n| coordinator | green |\n| aide | pink |\n| qa | yellow |\n| workers | blue |\n\n**Two ways to launch:**\n\n1. **One-call (preferred):** David opens a single `claude` in the project repo (inside tmux, fresh window) and invokes **`/coord-fleet [N]`**. That session cascades into the coordinator (invokes `/coordinator` itself), **infers the project name, agent ids, and `#room` from the repo basename** (sanitized to the id convention, collision-checked against live agents/rooms on the bus — it stops and asks David on any clash rather than squatting), then runs the launcher in `--self-coordinator` mode to scaffold aide/qa/workers around itself.\n2. **Script-direct:** run the launcher yourself from the agent-coordination repo:\n\n```bash\nscripts/coord-claude-layout.sh <N> --project=<name> --repo=<path> [--lanes=a,b,c] [--frame-only] [--self-coordinator] [--wait=s]\n```\n\nIt builds the window, styles the borders, launches `claude` in every pane, and injects each role's skill invocation (`/coordinator`, `/coord-aide`, `/coord-qa`, `/coord-worker` — all with the common `--id --role --project --room[s] --repo [--lane]` signature) plus its `/color`. Agent ids follow the `<project>-<role>` convention automatically.\n\nRules:\n\n- **Bootstrap starts with David.** Agents never scaffold a fleet on their own initiative — David either runs the script or invokes `/coord-fleet` in the one session he opened (his invocation *is* the authorization; sessions cost real money). After bootstrap, the coordinator onboards whatever appears on the bus.\n- **One fleet per project per machine.** The launcher refuses if ANY of the five role windows already exists (strict-create; the error names the kill commands). The console's spawn path instead reuses a role window whose panes are the fleet's own, and refuses on a foreign collision — never silent suffixing.\n- **`--frame-only`** builds panes + colors without launching sessions (for re-attaching existing agents or manual starts).\n- Workers' lanes default to `worker-i`; pass `--lanes=` when lane names are known up front, otherwise the coordinator assigns lanes at onboarding as usual.\n- **A seed that cannot name its agent must fail loudly, not start mute.** Any seeding path that templates an agent id — a hand-rolled prompt, a spawn script, a UI, anything other than the bundled launcher, which interpolates ids directly in shell and has no placeholder to leave behind — must **refuse to start** if a placeholder survives substitution. An unsubstituted id would be a *total, silent loss of outbound comms*: the agent binds no identity, so `send_message`/`post_status` are unavailable, while inbound still arrives over an existing pusher — it reads every instruction, can answer none, and presents to the coordinator as ordinary idleness. **Convert the convention into a loud failure** — an agent that cannot identify itself should refuse to run rather than run mute. *(Stated as a principle, not from a confirmed instance: the field case that motivated it — a worker mute for a whole session, 28 minutes of two lanes blocked — is established as **an agent started outside the standard path**, but the placeholder mechanism was a relayed self-report and no placeholder was ever found on disk. See LESSONS #34/#34b: the effect is evidence, the mechanism is not.)*\n\n<!-- §goal -->\n## Goal\n\nReduce raw chat load while keeping the benefits of multiple specialist agents:\n\n- repo owners keep implementation authority for their repos\n- reference agents review domain-specific risks\n- the coordinator keeps shared state, routes work, and prevents stale or duplicate asks\n- David receives compact decision packets instead of the full room firehose\n\n<!-- §role-model -->\n## Role Model\n\n| Agent | Role |\n| --- | --- |\n| Coordinator | **Executes: turns plans into routed work and gets them landed.** David's coordination layer and chief-of-staff. Filters room traffic, answers non-David questions, escalates real decisions, maintains the live board, and tracks quality/product/cutover risk. |\n| Repo owner | Owns one repository or service. Has implementation authority for that repo's branches, PRs, tests, deploy readiness, and local contract. |\n| Consumer owner | Owns the downstream consumer of another service. Reviews contract compatibility and user/product impact. |\n| Reference/advisory agent | Provides domain reference, source-system behavior, risk review, pricing/cost knowledge, or legacy implementation context. Does not mutate live production systems unless explicitly authorized. |\n| Infrastructure owner | Owns shared coordination tooling, chat delivery, CI/CD infrastructure, or deployment primitives. |\n| Aide | **Plans, in PRODUCT terms — what David is trying to achieve, for whom, what is worth doing next.** David's comms point — the one agent David talks to. Forwards the coordinator's decision packets to David; **curates** `docs/QUEUE.md` (priority/wording/scope — the coordinator closes items) and owns the roadmap; turns David's asks into queued items or roadmap phases. Quiet channel; never executes code. (Skill: `/coord-aide`.) |\n| QA / reviewer | **Validates quality AND challenges the choices — the only role chartered to contradict a plan, which is a different duty from gating a diff.** Standing independent quality gate. Listens for `DONE:`, runs the gate, issues cited PASS/FAIL verdicts. Reviews others' code, never its own; with a CI operator present it never merges. (Skill: `/coord-qa`.) |\n| CI operator | **Executes the pipeline and judges nothing — it merges on a verdict someone else issued.** Zero-judgment executor on a **cheap model**. Executes merges on QA's PASS verdicts, squash-verifies, watches the merge→qa deploy, posts telemetry, chases tier-2. Bounces all judgment (conflicts→worker, red pipelines→coordinator, prod→David). (Skill: `/coord-ci`.) |\n| Architecture auditor | On-demand, **read-only measurement** instrument. Checks the tree against DECISIONS/ARCHITECTURE_GUIDE/STACK_MAP (rule conformance), reports mechanical duplication/boundary/leftover findings, docs-vs-code drift, and friction stats from bus+git — cited, to the coordinator (queue candidates). **Does not judge whether the architecture is good**; design opinions go to David as questions. Never fixes, gates, or merges. (Skill: `/coord-audit`.) |\n| Automation (`groundwork-console`) | Mechanical watcher. Detects seam/bus events and may `send_message` with a playbook prefix (`FYI:` / `AGENT_ACTION:` / `RISK:`). Never edits seam files, never gates, never merges. Frozen role id `automation` — not a gate-runner, cannot emit `verdict` / `go` / `scope`. |\n| `david` | Human owner. Decides on authority, credentials, production risk, scope, priorities, and process changes. |\n\n<!-- §roles -->\n## Aide, QA & CI Roles\n\nThree specialist roles peel load off the coordinator's busiest seams — the David-facing channel, the quality gate, and the release pipeline. **All are optional:** a small project runs without them and the coordinator absorbs the jobs. Each ships as its own skill (`/coord-aide`, `/coord-qa`, `/coord-ci`) and defers to this playbook for the shared bus/room/prefix/noise protocol, so the skills stay thin. *(The aide has been renamed twice — \"backlog curator\" → \"liaison\" → **aide**, each time because the name pulled agents toward the wrong half of the job: \"curator\" read as queue clerk, \"liaison\" read as pure relay and understated the planning partnership. Running fleets may still hold `<project>-curator` or `<project>-<owner>-liaison` ids until restart; the aide answers to all three, and self-migrates with `rename_agent` per §*Agent Naming*.)*\n\n<!-- §aide -->\n### Aide — David's comms point & planning buddy\n\nThe aide is the **one agent David talks to** — his comms point and planning buddy, his **delegate** with a deliberately narrow surface. The division with the coordinator is by **facing, not content**: the aide faces David; the coordinator faces the fleet and organizes the work. (The earlier content split gave both roles a David-facing mandate and produced real turf fights — LESSONS #16.)\n\n- **Comms topology — `David ↔ aide ↔ coordinator ↔ fleet`.** All *conversational* agent→David traffic flows through the aide: the coordinator composes `DAVID_DECISION:` packets and DMs them to the **aide**, which forwards to `david` **verbatim** (the UI still parses the card; planning context goes around the packet, never inside it). Questions, reports expecting a reply, priority discussions — same path. Exactly **two sanctioned bypasses**: (1) **BLOCKER fast-path** — production-fire `BLOCKER:` goes coordinator→David directly (latency + single-point-of-failure safety), cc the aide; (2) **dock telemetry** — non-interrupting `RISK:`/`DONE:` dock DMs go coordinator→David's UI directly: a notification feed, not conversation; relaying it would make the aide the noise sink.\n- **Noise gradient — coordinator loud, aide quiet.** *(Prose on purpose. This rule already existed, was well-reasoned, and still failed to bind — and no mechanism was found that distinguishes a digest from a relay without reading the message. Recorded as a deliberate decision under ADR-014 rather than left as an item nobody mechanized.)* The **coordinator is the noise sink**: it watches the rooms and absorbs fleet chatter. The **aide is the quiet channel**: it gets filtered digests from the coordinator, not the room firehose, so David's messages never compete with fleet traffic. It may read the project room passively/on-demand (peer cross-correction stays valuable) but does not monitor it.\n- **David's inbound asks default to the aide** — planning *and* execution. Planning it handles; execution it forwards to the coordinator (normally as a Queue item; urgent → a tagged direct DM). Delegate, not bottleneck: forward fast, never sit on execution asks.\n- **What it owns:** `docs/QUEUE.md` (the inbound queue file) and the roadmap. **Minor** ask → a Queue item; **major** → open/plan a roadmap phase and reference it from the Queue (the human-facing front of the `plan-phase → BACKLOG` planner seam).\n- **It is David's proxy for the queue — but ownership splits by ACTION, not by file.** Assigning the *file* to one role left the verb `prune` with no owner at all, and the cost was measured: four merged items sat open and **twelve merges went 23 hours unlogged in `docs/DONE.md`**, because each writer could reasonably read the other as responsible. Note the mechanism, which is the transferable part — the coordinator read both rules, could not reconcile them, and resolved it *by doing less*. **A wrong rule gets challenged; a contradiction gets absorbed silently.** So:\n  - **AIDE curates** — priority, wording, whether an item belongs in the queue at all, whether it is really one item. It is David's proxy for *what the queue says*.\n  - **COORDINATOR closes** — prunes items a merge has satisfied, sets item status, writes `docs/DONE.md`. It sees merges land, so closing is a consequence of landing rather than a thing anyone must notice.\n  - **With no coordinator in the fleet, the aide does both.** State the fallback or it becomes the same unowned verb one role down; a fleet with an aide and no coordinator is common (it is how most start).\n  - Still one writer per *edit*: neither role rewrites the other's field on the same item. Write atomically and re-read before writing.\n  (David's ruling, 2026-08-22, re-ruled 2026-08-26.)\n- **It plans and relays; it does not execute.** The aide never owns a code lane, opens a *code* worktree, or merges. One writer to David's attention, one writer to the Queue; the coordinator drains in parallel.\n- **Narrow interface — the aide is not a routing target for the fleet.** Inbound: David and the coordinator. Outbound: David, the coordinator, and the queue/roadmap files — nothing else. Workers and QA do **not** @-mention or DM the aide; findings flow **worker/QA → coordinator → (filtered) → aide**, the coordinator deduping and filtering before anything reaches the queue.\n- **Route-once — one path per queue candidate:** **coordinator → aide**, exactly once; the coordinator's relay is *authoritative, not redundant*; workers and QA surface a candidate to the coordinator and stop. Dual-path routing produced duplicated tokens and crossed queue writes in the field — LESSONS #15.\n- **Lane disputes between aide and coordinator go to David as ONE joint decision packet** — never competing DMs. The aide's authority is David's channel and the queue; the coordinator's is the fleet and the board — and the board is a WRITE authority: `docs/WORKSTREAMS.md` is the coordinator's file and nobody else writes it.\n- **Deputized mode — explicit, temporary execution.** Under deadline pressure David may direct the aide to do hands-on work itself (install runtimes, write seed scripts, probe APIs). That is a feature, not a violation, *when it is explicit and temporary*: only on David's direct instruction; the aide announces `AGENT_ACTION: deputized — <task>` in the project room so the coordinator knows the lane exception exists; it still never merges, runs the gate, or takes a code lane on the coordinator's board; a `mission refresher` (or task completion) returns it to planning-only. Undirected drift into execution remains a role violation.\n\n<!-- §qa -->\n### QA — the quality gate\n\nThe QA agent is a standing, independent reviewer that turns the quality gate into a role instead of a coordinator chore.\n\n- **What it does:** listens for cited `DONE:` completions, runs the gate (typecheck + build + the real test suite + an independent behavior check against real input + a scope / `.skip` / `.only` audit + security-critical paths), and issues a **cited PASS/FAIL verdict**. With a CI operator present, **the verdict is QA's whole output — ci executes the merge**; on FAIL it reports to the coordinator, which routes back to the owning worker.\n- **Independence is the invariant: whoever merges did not author the change.** QA reviews workers' code, never its own. With ci holding the merge button, the separation is *structural*: QA never merges, so it may fix trivial nits freely without a forfeiture dance.\n- **Without a CI operator (fallback rules):** QA merges on pass — and then the forfeiture rule applies: touch the code (even a nit) and QA loses merge authority on that PR; the coordinator or a second reviewer merges. No QA at all → the coordinator runs the gate itself.\n- **Verdict freshness:** a PASS is bound to the PR head it reviewed — new commits void it (ci checks `headRefOid` before executing).\n- **The gate is single-threaded by design, so let the queue grow rather than lower the bar.** One QA agent gating 34 PRs in a day *is* the critical path, and a deep queue creates real pressure toward lighter passes — which is the one economy that destroys the role's entire value. The standing instruction is explicit: **let the queue grow rather than drop the standard.** Depth is scaled by *risk* (see *Scope* below), never by backlog length. If the queue is genuinely the constraint, that is a `DAVID_DECISION:` about a second gate agent — not a quiet relaxation of the gate. (The same run's five FAILs were all real, and all caught by checks QA introduced mid-session — LESSONS #25.)\n- **A PASS may not carry an author-actionable advisory — if the first line is a hold, the verdict is a hold.** \"PASS, but please fix X before merge\" reads as PASS to the ci operator and to every\n  parser; the advisory silently ships (field report §28). If the finding needs the author, the verdict is\n  FAIL (or PASS-HOLD where merge≠deploy); if it does not, put it after the verdict as an\n  observation, explicitly non-blocking. One verdict, one meaning.\n- **Gate-split once a real CI pipeline runs the suite on the PR head.** Where `ci` already runs typecheck, build and the full suite against the PR head on a cold runner, QA re-running it locally pays twice **and pays for the weaker environment** — a warm, pre-seeded dev tier structurally cannot exercise a bootstrap path. So with CI present, QA's default is: **require CI green, then spend the gate on what CI structurally cannot do** — judgement, scope-vs-contract, security paths, the independent behaviour check. The full local suite **stays mandatory** for schema/migrations, auth, money, and anything QA judges risky. **Every verdict states its mode** — `mode: ci-trusted` or `mode: full-local` — so a skipped suite is never ambiguous between policy and omission. **Prerequisite, non-negotiable:** a CI green is only as good as the commit it ran against. The measured bootstrap-path case: `EVIDENCE.md`.\n- **Scope:** routine, behavior-identical, low-risk PRs go straight to `main` — and the coordinator may take them off your queue entirely via the *Express lane* below (you audit those post-merge). **Money / fraud / auth / migration / high-risk surfaces still take the full fan-out gate** (off-bus adversarial auditor + pre-studying secondary — see *Money & High-Risk Review Gate*); QA alone is not sufficient there, the coordinator orchestrates that gate, and **enabling live money is always David's**.\n\n<!-- §ci -->\n### CI — the release pipeline operator (cheap model)\n\nThe CI operator executes the release path so neither QA nor the coordinator burns expensive context on mechanics. **Run it on a cheap model (Haiku-class)** — the role is designed to contain zero judgment: every duty is a lookup, an execution, or a classification, and anything that feels like a decision gets bounced.\n\n- **Executes, never decides:** on QA's cited PASS verdict (current-head only), after checking the coordinator's deploy holds → squash-merge, squash-verify (`git show origin/main:<path>`), watch the tier-1 deploy to qa, smoke-check, post `DONE:`/`RISK:` dock telemetry, log deploy state to FACTS. Chases tier-2 (nightly/E2E/scans) results; failures go to the coordinator as queue candidates.\n- **Hard bounces:** merge conflicts → the owning worker (ci never resolves them); red pipeline beyond one known-flaky re-run → classify (build|test|infra) and `BLOCKER:` the coordinator with the log pointer; fix-forward vs hold → coordinator; anything prod → David; quality → QA, always.\n- **Non-author by construction:** ci never writes code, so every merge it executes satisfies the non-author invariant automatically.\n- **Fallback:** no ci → QA merges under the forfeiture rules above; no QA either → coordinator.\n\n<!-- §express -->\n### Express lane — routine PRs bypass QA\n\nQA is single-threaded and its bar does not move with queue depth, so on a busy fleet the verdict queue *is* the critical path. The express lane takes the PRs that never needed a behavior check off that queue **without lowering the bar for anything that does**: the coordinator classifies at routing time, ci verifies eligibility mechanically and merges, QA audits after the fact.\n\n- **The coordinator decides, once, in the contract.** Every GO carries `gate: full` (default) or `gate: express`. Express is for changes whose risk is exhausted by typecheck + tests + PR-level CI: docs / copy / comments, config values, tests-only, behavior-identical refactors, dependency-free small fixes. **Never express:** auth · money · migrations / schema · dependency manifests / lockfiles · CI workflows · infra / k8s / Dockerfiles · secrets paths · anything the contract cannot describe as behavior-identical. When unsure → `full`. The tag is judgment, so it lives with the coordinator; nobody downstream re-decides it.\n- **The worker addresses an express `DONE:` to ci** (still a cited PR, PR checks green, same completion-report rules). A worker cannot self-promote to express — no tag in the contract means `full`.\n- **ci verifies eligibility with lookups only, then executes.** In order: the contract says `express` (quote the GO) · `headRefOid` current · PR checks green · `mergeable` · no deploy hold · `gh pr view --json files,additions,deletions`: no file under a deny path (`**/migrations/**`, `package.json`, `*lock*`, `.github/workflows/**`, `**/auth/**`, `**/*secret*`, `Dockerfile*`, `k8s/**`, `infra/**`), total churn ≤ 150 lines · `gh pr diff` adds no `.skip(`/`.only(`. **Every check passes → squash-merge → squash-verify → telemetry tagged `express`.** **Any check fails → not a bounce: forward the `DONE:` to QA as an ordinary full-lane item** (`FYI:` the coordinator with the failing check). ci never argues eligibility; a miss just falls back to the normal gate.\n- **An express commit that touches a package's `files` list, deletes source, or changes what a build emits names its `npm pack --dry-run` result in the self-check line** (file count + the specific presence/absence the change claims). A behavior-identical claim about a *shipped artifact* is only checkable on the artifact — the repo-level pack gate covers one tarball unless the kit extends it; QA's post-merge audit verified kit b27f729 (templates un-shipped, dead `dist/ids.js`) by hand, and found the author's stale `dist/` would have shipped the \"deleted\" file on the next publish (LESSONS #39).\n- **QA audits, never blocks.** QA reads express telemetry and spot-checks a sample post-merge (all of them when its queue is idle). A bad express merge is a `RISK:` to the coordinator, which stops tagging that class — the lane tightens by evidence, never by ci or QA opinion.\n- **Invariants untouched:** merge is still non-author (ci), routing is still single-router, QA's full-lane bar is unchanged, nothing new reaches David. Fallbacks: no ci → express PRs go to QA like everything else (QA runs the mechanical list instead of the worktree ritual, forfeiture still applies); no QA → coordinator.\n- *Server note (coord-mcp):* `ci` is not a gate-runner role, so a `DONE:` addressed to ci queues silently instead of push-waking the pane; ci's `wait_for_message` loop still picks it up promptly. Do not add `ci` to the gate-runner set to fix this — that would grant it verdict authority.\n\n<!-- §rooms -->\n## Rooms\n\n**An agent works in its project room, `#<project>`, and nowhere else** — routing, GOs, reports, blockers, onboarding, handover, presence. A fleet runs its entire life in one room, and cross-project asks go coordinator↔coordinator as DMs.\n\n**`#general` is retired: do not join, post, or route to it.** It was narrowed twice first — cross-project traffic only, then no default membership — and each time the coordinators stayed and their presence pings followed, until it became the thing it was scoped to avoid. **Scoping a shared channel by its intended CONTENT did not hold; only removing the reason to be in it did.** The default channel still exists: the server refuses to delete it, and David does not read it.\n\n| Room | Purpose |\n| --- | --- |\n| `#<project>` | **The coordinator's and its workers' primary working room.** All routing, GOs, completion reports, status diffs, blockers, and onboarding for that project happen here. Create it with `join_room`; set its topic on first join so other agents see what it is for. |\n| `#general` | **Retired — do not join.** The bus's default channel; it cannot be deleted, and nothing routes through it. Cross-project traffic goes coordinator↔coordinator as DMs. |\n| `#ops` | Terraform, deploys, namespace/RBAC, keys, tokens, CI runners, and cutover gates — when those span projects or warrant a shared lane. |\n| `#infra` | Shared tooling or coordination infrastructure, when it is noisy enough to deserve a separate lane. |\n\nGuidelines:\n\n- Work happens in the project room. **Cross-fleet asks travel coordinator↔coordinator as DMs** (§*Agent Naming & Multi-Owner Rooms*) — the only standing cross-project path, and it was already the sanctioned one.\n- Onboarding hands each agent `--rooms=<project>` only. An agent that finds itself in `#general` leaves with `leave_room`; being delivered its traffic is not a reason to answer there.\n- The board is `docs/WORKSTREAMS.md` — repo-local, so coordinators on different projects never collide even though the bus is shared (no per-project filename suffix needed). Don't let dead rooms accumulate: leftover rooms become cross-fleet routing surfaces, which is what `#general` became.\n\n<!-- §rooms-orientation -->\n### Orientation artifacts (topic / MOTD) are owned, and they assert *location*, not *state*\n\nA joining agent's whole orientation is `join` → **default-room MOTD** → `join_room` → **room topic + MOTD** → history. These are the **first things it reads and the last things anyone reviews** — they sit outside every gate the fleet has, they are read before the agent has any repo context to check them against, and a wrong one misinforms *every* future join, not once (LESSONS #31). Ownership therefore applies to them exactly as to repo files (§*Board Accuracy Rules*, LESSONS #21):\n\n- **Name an owner in the artifact itself** — `Topic owner: <agentId>` — and treat topic/MOTD edits as reviewable changes, not housekeeping. Unowned is how they rot: the room's creator stops seeing them as information and starts seeing them as furniture.\n- **Assert where things live, never lifecycle state.** `board: docs/WORKSTREAMS.md · queue: docs/QUEUE.md · coordinator: <id>` stays true for a project's whole life. `\"fresh repo, no board docs yet\"`, `\"Phase 1 MVP\"`, `\"integration branch: feature/phase14\"` are **guaranteed to become lies** and were found doing so in live rooms — one told every joining agent that no planning docs existed for a repo with 961 commits and six board documents, shaping its first move against the truth.\n- **An id in a topic is a routing instruction, so re-check it after any rename.** Topics naming a coordinator that has since self-renamed (`bf-coord` → `bf-david-coord`) point new agents at an id that no longer exists — worse than a stale doc claim, because it fails as an *instruction*. Rename an agent, audit the rooms that name it (§*Agent Naming*).\n- **Cross-project artifacts are David's, not a coordinator's to rewrite.** `#general`'s MOTD is served as `defaultRoom` to **every** agent on `join`, across all projects — retiring the room does not change that, since `join` returns it whether or not anyone is a member — so a coordinator that \"just fixes\" it silently rewrites another fleet's onboarding. Flag drift to David with a proposed replacement; never edit it unilaterally. (Found stale in the field: it named three focused rooms, one of which **did not exist** and one of which had been dead for months, while omitting every currently-active project room.)\n- **Keep the MOTD small enough to correct, and put the doctrine in a repo file.** An MOTD is read on every join, so the temptation is to put everything in it — but a large one becomes *unaffordable to fix*, and then it goes stale in place. Measured: one room's MOTD reached **33,870 bytes** while every other room on the bus sat at 0–739; a rule routing escalations to a role David had just deleted was left standing there because another 34KB rewrite \"wasn't worth one stale clause\". Doctrine belongs in a versioned repo file (`docs/BUS_PROTOCOL.md`), with the MOTD reduced to a **pointer plus whatever changes behaviour right now** — live suspensions, the current gate rule, where the board and queue live. `set_room_motd` takes `motdAppend` and `motdPatch:{find,replace}` precisely so a one-clause correction costs one small call; past ~4KB it warns and names this pattern. A stale rule in a big MOTD outranks a maintained file, because the MOTD is what a joining agent reads first.\n- **Absent beats wrong, but neither is fine.** A room with no topic gives a joining agent nothing; a stale one gives it a confident falsehood it has no way to check. Set the topic on room creation (§*Rooms* table) and re-read it whenever you cite it — reading your own topic in a `list_rooms` dump does not count as reviewing it.\n\n**The audit unit is every artifact that RESOLVES AN ID, not every artifact that mentions one** (LESSONS #31b). Four artifacts resolve ids — room **topic**, room **MOTD**, room **membership**, and the **agent registry** — and they can disagree with each other silently. The severity ordering is what matters: prose naming a dead id *misinforms a reader*, who can notice; **membership and the registry make an id addressable**, so an agent routes to it in good faith and gets **silence rather than an error** — a DM lands in an inbox no process reads. Found live: two agents listed as members of a project room were **absent from the registry entirely**, and a fleet whose *rename* audit was genuinely clean still had three defects in this class.\n\n- **Reconcile membership against the registry — the sweep is free.** `ping { from, to }` answers entirely server-side (zero model tokens on the target) and returns `reason: \"unregistered\"` for a phantom, so every member of every room can be checked for the cost of a few calls. This was never a hard check, only an unrun one: ping each room member, and anything `unregistered` is a routing black hole to clear.\n- **Detection and remediation have different reliability — never let one lesson fuse them.** `ping` *detects* a phantom reliably and for free. **Removing it is a separate operation that must be verified on its own terms**, and the built-in sweep is not known to close what the probe opens: a field dry-run of `prune {room, targets:[\"members\"]}` reported `orphanMembers: []` on a room holding **two members `ping` had just called `unregistered`** (LESSONS #32). So: probe with `ping`, remediate deliberately, then **re-probe to confirm the removal**. A sweep returning `[]` is not evidence the class is clean — it may be evidence the sweep cannot see the defect.\n- **Registration fields are unvalidated, which is *why* they drift.** `role` is free text, so one fleet carried `role: \"worker-4\"` on one worker while its siblings had `role: \"worker\"` (an instance number where the others hold a class — harmless until something filters by role), and two live agents had **no `role` at all**. Nothing rejects any of it. Treat your own `join { agentId, role, project }` as an artifact you own: role is the **class**, the instance number lives in the id.\n- **Audit the class, not the instance you were asked about.** The fleet above passed the rename check and would have reported \"clean\" had it only checked what was asked — the three defects surfaced because it inspected the whole artifact class instead. When one member of an unowned class is found rotten, sweep the others.\n\n<!-- §naming -->\n## Agent Naming & Multi-Owner Rooms\n\n**Agent ID convention: `<project>-<owner>-<role>[-n]`** (e.g. `bf-david-aide`,\n`bf-marco-worker-2`). `owner` is the fleet's human sponsor — the person whose\n`DAVID_DECISION:`-class escalations this fleet routes to. Adopted 2026-07-08 when\nproject rooms became multi-owner: two developers can connect their fleets to the\nsame `#<project>` room, and attribution must be readable from the ID alone.\n`coord-claude-layout.sh --owner=<name>` bakes it in (defaults to `$USER`).\n\nLegacy `<project>-<role>` IDs self-migrate: each agent calls `rename_agent` on\nITSELF (the caller's token binding rotates — never rename another agent), then\nre-attaches its transport (`attach_agent`; rename detaches tmux-push).\n\n**Multi-owner authority rule:** a worker acts only on `GO:` from its **own\nowner's** coordinator. Cross-fleet asks travel coordinator↔coordinator as DMs —\nnever directly to another owner's workers, and never as room broadcasts that\ncould read as tasking. Silence from a foreign coordinator is not permission.\nEach owner's aide faces only its own owner; there is no cross-owner\naide↔aide lane (owners talk to each other as humans).\n\n<!-- §bus-prefixes -->\n## Message Prefixes\n\nAgents should prefix important room messages with one of these:\n\n- `FYI:` no action needed\n- `AGENT_ACTION:` another agent can handle this without David\n- `DAVID_DECISION:` David must decide\n- `BLOCKER:` work cannot continue without an action or decision\n- `RISK:` quality, security, production, cost, or product risk\n- `DONE:` completed work or closed item\n\nThe coordinator may ask agents to restate unclear messages using these prefixes.\n\n**The prefix is for the human eye; `record.type` is the one the bus reads — and every agent→agent message carries one.** The nine types are `decision · verdict · done · blocker · risk · fyi · action · go · scope`, and they map onto the prefixes above one-for-one (`AGENT_ACTION:` → `action`, `DAVID_DECISION:` → `decision`; `GO:`/`SCOPE:` are the coordinator's two). Send both:\n\n```\nsend_message { from, to, text: \"DONE: task 12 landed — …\",\n               record: { type: \"done\", payload: { summary: \"…\" },\n                         cites: [{ kind: \"pr\", ref: \"owner/repo#163\" }] } }\n```\n\n- **`text` is untouched by the record and your wording always wins** — a record renders into `text` only when you supplied none.\n- **Why it is obligatory rather than encouraged:** a typed multi-line message is delivered as ONE attributed line plus a `retrieve_message` handle; an untyped one arrives **in full, in every reader's context**, and its continuation lines arrive with no `[tag time from]` header at all, so a reader cannot even attribute them. Measured on one room: 206 messages, 175 multi-line, 33 typed — the slimming shipped and went unused for days.\n- **An untyped agent→agent send is refused at the SEND, not the render** (`agent-coord-mcp` ≥0.26.10; WARN with the date named until **2026-09-15**, REFUSE after). Enforcing where the message is read would leave the untyped message on disk and the next reader re-deriving its type from prose. The refusal names the type you should have used and the literal call that succeeds.\n- **`fyi` is the honest catch-all.** If nothing fits, it is `fyi` — do not force a false `decision`/`risk` to get past the gate. A mistyped record is worse than an untyped one, because the type is then noise nobody can query.\n- **David-facing messages stay prose.** The rule is scoped to agent→agent traffic; a message whose recipient holds a human role is exempt by construction, and needs no flag.\n- **A model that cannot reliably pick a type declares `proseOnly: true` at `join`** — per agent, never a global env var, visible and counted in `list_agents`. **The exemption is granted to the SENDER and paid by every READER:** an untyped message cannot be slimmed, so a prose-only agent spends *other* agents' context on every multi-line send. That is why it is opt-in and reviewed rather than self-service, and why a rising exempt share is the number that says the rule is decaying.\n\n**Every `DONE:` must cite its PR** — a URL, `owner/repo#N`, or `PR #N` when the channel has a default repo. This is what lets the coordinator (or an automated claim-verifier) confirm merge state from `gh` instead of trusting the message. A `DONE:` with no PR reference is unverifiable and should be treated as not-yet-done until cited.\n\n**Degraded comms: lead with the blocker, not the deliverable.** If your only channel out is narrow or borrowed — you can receive but not transmit, your bus tools are unavailable, you are relaying through a human — the *first* line must be the constraint and the ask, never the work product. An agent that reported its finished push to David but buried \"please relay this\" mid-message stayed blocked, and two other lanes with it, because **a constraint nobody acts on is indistinguishable from silence** (LESSONS #34). Say `BLOCKER: cannot transmit — relay to <coordinator>: <one line>` first; the deliverable goes underneath.\n\n<!-- §bus-relay -->\n## Relay Authenticity\n\nAgents are (rightly) trained to treat unexpected mid-task instruction text as potential prompt injection — which means a *legitimate* scope change relayed over the bus can be silently discarded as suspicious. This happened in the field: a sub-agent dropped real coordinator corrections and cost a full re-send cycle. Right instinct, wrong outcome. The fix is a provenance convention:\n\n- **The coordinator countersigns relayed scope changes.** A mid-task instruction that amends a worker's contract arrives as a coordinator DM that leads with **`SCOPE CHANGE:`** (or `SCOPE:`) and references the contract it amends. The explicit prefix plus the known coordinator sender id is the countersignature — and under tiered delivery (coord-mcp ≥v0.12.0) that same prefix from a trusted sender is what makes the relay push immediately instead of queueing.\n- **Prefer file + pointer for instruction-bearing relays.** Write the amended contract to a repo file (ideally the contract's existing file) and DM a short pointer. Repo-file provenance reads as data, not as mid-stream injected instructions — and it composes with the long-contract rule below.\n- **Workers:** an instruction arriving as a countersigned coordinator DM, or as a pointer to a contract file in the repo, is authentic by convention — verify the sender id, then act on it. If an instruction-bearing relay arrives with *neither* marker, don't silently drop it: ask the coordinator to confirm in one line.\n- **Never start a message with `/`.** The tmux pusher's injection guard stores leading-slash text in the inbox but never types it into a pane, so `/status …` as a DM reaches no one's screen (`send_message` now warns). Say `AGENT_ACTION: run /<skill> …`; only `send_command` (`/clear`, `/compact`, `/reload-skills`) goes in raw.\n\n<!-- §coord-duties -->\n## Coordinator Duties\n\nThe coordinator acts as David's channel and second-in-command:\n\n- answer questions that do not require David\n- route repo-specific work to the responsible repo owner\n- ask for review from the most relevant non-author agent\n- detect and correct stale room state\n- prevent cross-checkout and cross-repo contamination\n- maintain a concise live state board\n- escalate only real David decisions, with context and a recommendation\n- restate David's decisions back to the room so all agents align\n\n<!-- §coord-execute -->\n## How To Execute The Coordinator Role\n\nThe coordinator's job is not to do every task. The job is to keep the system coherent so specialist agents can move quickly without turning David into the message bus.\n\nOperating posture:\n\n- Be the single routing point for cross-agent ambiguity.\n- Trust repo owners on repo facts, but verify claims that affect decisions, merges, deploys, spend, or production risk.\n- Keep implementation authority with the owning agent unless David reassigns it.\n- Prefer short, decisive room messages over long discussion threads.\n- Collapse noisy debate into a small number of options and a recommendation.\n- Keep David out of routine execution, but bring him in early for irreversible, costly, credentialed, production, or ownership decisions.\n\nStartup loop:\n\n1. Register or join as the coordinator identity.\n2. Attach live message delivery and confirm it is working.\n3. Join the relevant focused rooms.\n4. Read or reconstruct the live board, and read the project queue (`docs/QUEUE.md`; legacy `docs/BACKLOG.md`) for queued work.\n5. Announce coordinator state in the **project room**: active, rooms joined, current blockers, and how agents should route requests.\n6. If replacing another coordinator, wait for David's explicit handoff decision and the outgoing coordinator's handover packet.\n\nDaily operating loop:\n\n1. Watch the **project room** for David decisions, blockers, stale routing, and unclear ownership. Cross-project traffic arrives as a coordinator↔coordinator DM, not from a shared room.\n2. Keep detailed implementation discussion in focused rooms.\n3. Convert ambiguous messages into one of: `AGENT_ACTION`, `DAVID_DECISION`, `BLOCKER`, `RISK`, `DONE`, or `FYI`.\n4. When a lane has capacity: `next_unblocked` → `claim` → route it as a contract; `land` when it merges (§*Bus Verbs*).\n5. Route work to the owning agent, with the expected output and merge/review gate.\n6. Ask the most relevant non-author agent for review when risk warrants it.\n7. Update the live board when work merges, blocks, or changes owner.\n8. Correct stale board state quickly and visibly, especially when an item is already merged, deployed, blocked on ops, or no longer relevant.\n9. Send David compact decision packets only when the room cannot safely proceed without him.\n\nWhen a new or replacement agent joins:\n\n1. Confirm the agent's role, repo lane, and rooms.\n2. Onboard it with `/coord-worker --rooms=<project>` so it reports in the project room; add extra rooms only if its lane genuinely spans them.\n3. Point it to this playbook and the current live board.\n4. Summarize only the state needed for its lane.\n5. State explicit boundaries: repo ownership, branch/PR expectations, secrets policy, and production guardrails.\n6. Give one concrete next action or tell it to stay idle/on-call.\n7. Ask for an ACK so delivery and comprehension are confirmed.\n\n<!-- §context-topology -->\n## Context Topology & Delegation Economics\n\nThe system is hub-and-spoke for *context*, not just routing. Getting the topology right is what keeps the whole fleet's token cost sub-linear.\n\n- **Asymmetric context is the design, not an accident.** The coordinator is the one **wide, persistent** context that holds the global picture *once*; workers are **narrow, ephemeral** spokes that see only their current slice and get cleared between tasks. Delegation is the *mechanism* that keeps spokes lean — a worker never needs the map, so its context never bloats. Resist the pull to brief everyone on everything.\n- **The board is the coordinator's swap-space, and its SOLE WRITER is the coordinator.** The coordinator offloads global state to a durable board (`docs/WORKSTREAMS.md` — repo-local; a bus-side board later) so its own window stays lean. Every other role reads it and never writes it — queue and done carry that never-clause explicitly and the board carried none, which left an agent looking at a stale row with no prohibition to stop it. Board is the **state**; chat is the **audit log of transitions**. Write state to the **project room**. An empty board plus a bloated room is the anti-pattern.\n- **Delegation floor — delegate substantial slices, do trivial work inline.** Delegation has a fixed tax: writing a self-contained contract plus a review round-trip. If that tax exceeds the work being handed off, delegating is net-negative — just do it inline. Reserve delegation for slices big enough to repay the coordination cost.\n- **The contract is a compression interface, not bureaucracy.** A sharp, self-contained task contract (goal, inputs, boundaries, done-definition, gate) is precisely what *buys* the lean executor: the tighter the contract, the less context the worker needs, the harder it can be cleared afterward. Vague contracts force the worker to carry (and re-derive) context it should never have held.\n- **Keep a per-lane work queue so spokes never idle.** Routing is not \"coordinator hands out one task at a time on request.\" Maintain a ready next-GO per lane so a worker pulls the next slice the instant one lands (see *Worker Flow: No Idle Gaps*).\n\n<!-- §audit -->\n## Architecture Audit (structural drift)\n\nEvery standing role sees a slice: the coordinator holds the board, workers hold a lane, QA holds one PR, docs hold *intent*. **Nobody re-derives whether the code still matches the architecture that was decided** — so duplication, boundary leaks and silently violated ADRs accumulate below every gate's resolution until they surface as the bug no agent can fix in a codebase no human has read. The audit is the periodic instrument that looks (skill: `/coord-audit`).\n\n- **Read-only, report-only, on demand.** David or the coordinator invokes it (per phase close, per N merges, or when a smell recurs). It authors no code, opens no code PRs, issues no verdicts, and reports to the **coordinator only** — accepted findings become queue candidates the coordinator relays to the aide once (route-once).\n- **Measurement, not taste.** An agent reading agent-written code grades its surface and shares the writer's priors; maintainability has no oracle at read time (LESSONS *the same models* — the podcast's \"if the model knew what good code looked like it would write it\"). So the audit is confined to what is checkable: **(a) conformance** to stated rules, **(b) mechanical measurements** (duplication, forbidden imports, leftovers, size, churn), **(c) docs-vs-code disagreement**, **(d) friction stats** from bus + git (co-change clusters, churn, QA bounces per path, context resets per lane) — architecture cost measured by its consequences, the only honest quality signal. Design opinions are not findings; they go to David under *Questions*, with evidence, uncounted.\n- **Docs are the hypothesis, the tree is the evidence.** It reads DECISIONS/ARCHITECTURE_GUIDE/STACK_MAP/domain model first, turns each rule into a *falsifiable claim*, then checks the claims against a fresh `origin/main` worktree with positive controls (§*Verify Before You Report Or Assert*). Tripwires (dup/boundary lint, `groundwork doctor`) run first and are quoted raw. Findings are cited `file:line`, classified (`RULE-VIOLATION` · `DUPLICATION` · `BOUNDARY-IMPORT` · `LEFTOVER` · `DOC-DRIFT` · `TEST-CANNOT-FAIL` · `FRICTION`), severity by blast radius / measured cost, and **scoped to what was measured**. Uncovered areas are listed — silent partial coverage reads as clean.\n- **Drift cuts both ways.** \"Docs wrong, not code\" is a first-class finding; the fix is a doc/ADR update, not a code task.\n- **Accepted deviations are facts.** Anything David/the coordinator chooses to live with is written to `docs/FACTS.md` (with the audit SHA) so it is not re-reported; a finding that recurs across audits with no such fact is flagged `RECURRING` and treated as a **guard candidate** (see LESSONS *Guard* field) rather than another task.\n- Reports live in `docs/audits/<date>-<sha7>.md` (docs-only branch/PR).\n\n<!-- §board-queue -->\n## Task Backlog (Inbound Queue)\n\nThe board is the coordinator's *outbound* state (\"what's happening\"). The **backlog** is its *inbound* twin (\"what David wants next\") — a durable, David-owned queue that replaces ephemeral chat asks. Chat is a poor queue: unordered, no priority, buried in the firehose, and every ask wakes the whole bus. A file is append-anytime, prioritized, greppable, diff-able, and costs zero bus tokens.\n\n- **Location:** two files in each project repo — **`docs/QUEUE.md`** (inbound queue) and **`docs/DONE.md`** (completion log) — versioned, and David edits where the work lives. Per-project, like the board. **Legacy layout (single `docs/BACKLOG.md` with `## Queue`/`## Done` regions):** still parsed by the UI; existing projects migrate by a one-time mechanical split — this is the only normative mention; everywhere else, read \"queue/done files\" as covering both until migration completes.\n- **Single writer per ACTION (the file alone is not enough — see *Aide*):** `docs/QUEUE.md` is **David's file** for curation — written by David directly, by the **aide** as his proxy, or via an authorized editing surface (e.g. groundwork-console, formerly agent-coord-ui) acting on his behalf; those are the *same logical writer*. `docs/DONE.md` is the **coordinator's file, append-only**. One writer per ACTION means git and the filesystem arbitrate, and the shared-region CAS ceremony disappears (LESSONS #7). Pruning satisfied or merge-obsoleted Queue items is the **coordinator's obligation** — it sees merges land, so closing follows from landing rather than from someone noticing; with no coordinator, the aide does both.\n- **The queue feeds the board; it does not duplicate it.** Pulling a task makes it an info-dense contract and a 🚧 In Progress row in `docs/WORKSTREAMS.md` (`## Active Streams`) — `claim` writes that row. On completion `land` appends the `docs/DONE.md` line with its PR ref and closes the item in `docs/QUEUE.md` — status and pruning only, never priority or wording, which are the aide's. Live state lives on the board; the queue stays thin.\n- **How the coordinator drains it: `next_unblocked` answers \"what next\", `claim` opens the row, `land` closes it.** The ordering, the tie-break, the skip and the board hunk are the verb's job now (§*Bus Verbs*) — what stays a judgment call is converting the item into a contract (goal · boundaries · done-def · gate · cited refs) and choosing the lane. The queue is the **inbound swap-space**, mirroring the board as the outbound one: it lets the coordinator pull one item when there is capacity instead of holding all of David's intentions in context.\n- **Dependencies: the aide orders, the coordinator detects, one DM closes the loop.** The aide orders the queue without lane capacity or dependency knowledge; the coordinator sees both but cannot write the file. `next_unblocked` performs the skip and returns the board hunk that records it; the part no verb can do is the **one** `AGENT_ACTION: RESEQUENCE: <item> after <item> — <one-line why>` DM to the aide. Route-once applies: one path, one message, no re-asking.\n- **Format — the groundwork-console parser contract** (see the fleet writer rules under *Board Accuracy Rules*). Match it exactly or the UI BacklogPanel renders **empty** — silently, not an error (polywatch hit this; tolerance added in `agent-coord-ui#58`; split-file support in `agent-coord-ui#59`):\n  - **File precedence:** if `docs/QUEUE.md` or `docs/DONE.md` exists, the UI reads the split files; otherwise it falls back to legacy `docs/BACKLOG.md`. In the split files the `# QUEUE — <project>` / `# DONE — <project>` title and the `## Queue`/`## Done` h2 are optional — headerless item lines parse too — but keep the headers for readability.\n  - In the legacy layout, `## Queue` and `## Done` are the recognized h2 sections (**order-independent**); any other h2 section is ignored.\n  - **Queue item:** `- [ ] (P1) <task text>` — checkbox, then a **required** priority `(P1)`/`(P2)`/`(P3)` (parenthesized, or compact `[P1]` post-#58), then the task. The parser captures *everything* after the priority as task text — Queue refs are **not** separately extracted, so any `— refs` you add is just part of the displayed text, not a structured field.\n  - **Done item:** `- [x] <task> — <ref> · YYYY-MM-DD` — ref and date **are** parsed, and the separator glyphs are exact: the ref splits on the **last ` — `** (space + EM DASH U+2014 + space) and the date is a trailing ` · YYYY-MM-DD` (space + MIDDLE DOT U+00B7 + space). A plain hyphen `-` or ` - ` will **not** split the ref; any other date format will **not** extract. Use the exact glyphs.\n  - `### Subsection` (h3) headers are allowed inside `## Queue`/`## Done` for grouping. Everything else — prose, non-priority bracket tags (e.g. `[ops]`) — is ignored by the parser.\n\n```text\ndocs/QUEUE.md                                docs/DONE.md\n# QUEUE — <project>                          # DONE — <project>\n\n## Queue                                     ## Done\n- [ ] (P1) <task text>                       - [x] <task> — owner/repo#N · YYYY-MM-DD\n- [ ] (P2) <task text>\n```\n\n<!-- §facts -->\n## Fact Store (Shared World-Model)\n\nChat was the only shared world-model, and it drifted: agents restated repo state from memory, others built decision chains on it, and nobody could tell a verified claim from a confident guess (a whole design was once built on a feature flag that did not exist — LESSONS #5). The tiebreak hierarchy settles *disputes*; the fact store keeps the settled answer from re-drifting.\n\n**The artifact** is `docs/FACTS.md`, a Groundwork seam file (shipped groundwork#1, alongside QUEUE/DONE/WORKSTREAMS): one entry per fact — stable kebab-case id · claim · `verified: <timestamp> · by: <who> · method: <how>` (exact em-dash/middot glyphs, like the queue format). Write entries with the deterministic helper `docs/.groundwork/scripts/set-fact.mjs <id> \"<claim>\" --by <agentId> --method \"<how>\"` (atomic insert-or-replace + timestamp); `groundwork doctor` flags entries older than 14 days or missing their verification line.\n\n**The protocol** on the bus:\n\n- **Chat claims are hypotheses until they're in FACTS with a method.** A decision chain may only build on cited fact ids, never on world-state restated from memory. If it matters enough to build on, it matters enough to verify and write.\n- **Cite ids, don't restate.** Bus messages reference facts (`per FACTS: nightly-export-job`) instead of re-asserting the underlying claim — composes with the file+pointer default, and a wrong fact gets corrected in one place instead of chased through the room.\n- **One writer per fact: whoever verified it.** Conflicting verifications go through the tiebreak hierarchy (*Verify Before You Report Or Assert* — gh-API read of `origin/main` beats local checkout beats chat memory), and the winning read replaces the entry via `set-fact`.\n- **Staleness has an owner: ci.** Running `groundwork doctor` and reporting entries older than 14 days (or missing a verification line) is a lookup, so it rides the tier-2 chase — `FYI:` the stale ids to the coordinator, which routes re-verification to whoever can check it. ci never re-verifies a fact itself. An unrefreshed fact is a hypothesis again; decisions do not build on it.\n- **Scope:** operational world-state that agents act on (does X exist, is Y merged/deployed/enabled, inventory results). Not planning intent (queue), not live execution state (board), not cross-project lessons (knowledge repo).\n\n<!-- §context-reset -->\n## Context Reset Discipline\n\n**Managing each worker's context is the coordinator's responsibility, not the worker's.** The coordinator owns every worker's context budget: it keeps contracts tight so a worker never has to hold the global map, decides when to `/clear` vs `/compact` vs narrowly rehydrate, reseeds a switched worker with only the minimum state, and does not let unrelated work stack into a long-lived worker context when a clean reset is cheaper and safer.\n\nRules:\n\n- Do **not** mandate a `/clear` between related slices of the *same* task — clearing a worker mid-task destroys the context it needs and is a leading cause of idle gaps and stale-state confusion. Reserve `/clear` for a genuine task switch into a *materially different* lane.\n- **Clear/compact at boundaries, never at idle — it's a prompt-cache calculation.** A `/clear` throws away the cached prompt prefix. Clearing *then sitting idle* pays that cost and recovers nothing — a net loss. Clearing *before a long fresh run* amortizes it across many cheaper turns — a net win. So: `/clear` before assigning a meaningfully different multi-turn task; **never** `/clear` an idle finisher just to \"tidy up.\" Use `/compact` for a long but still-relevant thread.\n- When you do switch a worker to a different task, provide a fresh context seed with only the minimum state required: current goal, owner, relevant room, required files or PRs, and the next concrete action.\n- Do not rehydrate the entire room history unless the worker truly needs it — `read_messages` already windows to the recent slice and digests the rest, so a default read is bounded; expand specifics with `retrieve_room_history` rather than dumping full history into a seed.\n- Prefer **narrow rehydrate over reset**: a small, explicit context top-up keeps a worker moving where a clear would stall it.\n- Use the smallest amount of context that preserves correctness, then let the worker ask for more if it needs it.\n\n- **A recurring job's prompt outranks a fresh ruling — the copy fires automatically and the ruling has to be remembered.** Any long-lived scheduled prompt the kit ships carries a **say-so-and-re-arm** clause: it names *what to re-check* before acting — the specific documents, rulings or state its instructions depend on — and re-states its own assumptions in its output. **\"Check for changes\" is too vague to survive**, and a vague instruction is precisely the part that decays; a pattern without the clause fails review.\n<!-- §context-phase -->\n## Phase Boundaries\n\nA phase completing (`PHASE*_TASKS.md` checkboxes all ticked, then marked complete in the roadmap and recorded in `docs/DONE.md`) is a genuine task-switch for the fleet. The **coordinator** owns the boundary; workers do not self-clear and the console does not execute.\n\n1. **Handover snapshots first** — each affected worker emits the `coord-handover` three-liner (rooms, name, mission).\n2. **Run `/coord-audit`** on the just-closed phase (read-only; findings are queue candidates, not a gate).\n3. **Then `/clear`** workers whose next work is a *materially different* lane (`send_command`, never by asking). Re-seed from the snapshot + a new GO. Do not `/clear` an idle finisher that still owns the next slice in the same lane.\n\nA watcher (`groundwork-console`) may nudge this with `AGENT_ACTION:` to the coordinator. It never runs the audit or the clear itself.\n\n<!-- §context-history -->\n## History Retrieval\n\nRoom history is part of the system memory. The coordinator should treat it as a source of truth for recent decisions, ownership, and unresolved questions.\n\nRules:\n\n- Prefer retrieval from room history before asking an agent to restate what was already discussed.\n- If a question depends on prior context, search the history first and quote or summarize the relevant message instead of reconstructing from memory.\n- **Retrieval is native — don't scroll, don't reseed the whole channel.** `read_messages` returns the recent window plus a compact `history` digest of any older overflow (count, agents, time span, error posts) carrying a hash. Expand only what you need with `retrieve_room_history({hash, query})`; `query` does a substring search within that slice. This is the search-layer the older guidance described — it now ships, so no manual scrolling and no separate index for recent coordination work.\n- **Caveats:** a `history` hash is scoped to the agent that produced it (you can't expand another agent's read) and expires after 30 minutes — if it's gone, re-read the channel at a higher `limit`. `peek` shows the overflow count but yields no expandable hash.\n- When using retrieved history to make a decision, surface the exact source message or a short attribution so the room can verify the claim.\n- Use history retrieval to prevent duplicate asks, stale routing, and repeated handoffs.\n\n<!-- §bus-tokens -->\n## Token Economy & Noise Control\n\nTo prevent runaway token burns and eliminate chatter noise across the multi-agent bus:\n\nRules:\n\n- **No Conversational Acknowledgements:** Agents must never post conversational replies like \"Acknowledged\", \"Copy that\", or \"Aligned\". These messages trigger subsequent wake-ups and cause feedback loops. If confirmation is required, use silent state updates via `post_status` or remain quiet.\n- **File-Based Board Sync (Anti-Bloat):** Do not dump large markdown tables or live board states directly into chat channels. Instead, keep the board in the shared repo-local file (`docs/WORKSTREAMS.md`) and reference its URL in chat.
